extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism and religious/apologetic writers; educated public interested in standards for theological argument and public discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing sermons, apologetic manuals, and religious polemics for intellectual honesty, accuracy, and moral effect. Focuses on truthfulness, use of evidence, hermeneutics, rhetoric, and the ethical tone of religious teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference of truth requires cooperation of intellect and impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: “That highest moral habit, the constant preference of truth, both theoretically and practically, pre-eminently demands the co-operation of the intellect with the impulses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a writer or preacher balances emotion and reason. Warning: sects or writers that exalt feeling above intellect tend to have a 'misty and confused' sense of truthfulness (example: enthusiastic Methodists who accept stories because they accord with wishes). A strong work should show the intellect cooperating with religious impulses rather than being submerged by them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doctrines that imprison the intellect (verbal inspiration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine of verbal inspiration may ‘imprison the intellect, depriving it of its proper function—the free search for truth—and making it the mere servant-of-all-work to a foregone conclusion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether theological commitments force selective fact-finding (searching for facts that 'will bear out their doctrine'), reject direct evidence in favor of congenial indirect evidence, or resort to expedients to explain away contradictions. Such practices are anti-patterns that blunt perception and the sense of truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prefer 'readiness' to veracity; avoid 'ready replies' and superficial answers
rubrics_metrics.description: A work that aims chiefly to furnish a ‘ready reply’ or ‘change in their pocket’ sacrifices veracity for quick answers and may encourage giving ‘a foolish answer’ to a fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether answers are hurried, simplistic, or contrived for debating convenience rather than carefully evidenced. Examples: Dr. Cumming's 'Manual of Christian Evidences' is criticized for prioritizing readiness over truth and employing ready-made but inaccurate rejoinders and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address actual, contemporary difficulties; avoid strawmen and past-only objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that directs arguments against opinions 'either totally imaginary, or that belong to the past rather than to the present' fails to meet the difficulties actually felt by honest inquirers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the writer engages with modern historical criticism, contemporary moral objections, and the real positions of thinkers, rather than attacking fossilized or invented caricatures (example: recommending Leland’s 'short and easy method' and writing feebler versions of obsolete arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accuracy in quotations and anecdotes; vet sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid introducing apocryphal or grossly false stories and misattributed quotations (example: misattributing doggerel lines to Byron; repeating vulgar fables about Voltaire’s death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual accuracy of illustrative material and quotations. Anti-patterns include repeating hearsay, second-hand errors, and apocryphal anecdotes used as evidence. Reliable work checks sources and does not sacrifice accuracy for rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between fact and rhetoric/dramatic device
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatized or rhetorical reconstruction (e.g., a peasant’s speech) must be clearly signposted; ambiguity makes it impossible to judge truthfulness versus rhetorical invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity about whether a passage reports an actual utterance, a hypothetical/example, or a dramatic contrivance. Failure to distinguish undermines credibility and prevents assessment of honesty or judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid caricaturing and demonizing opponents; represent their views fairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting up grotesque 'creeds' of opponents (e.g., Dr. Cumming’s 'Creed of the Infidel') or treating whole groups as instruments of Satan misrepresents and dehumanizes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author fairly presents opponents' beliefs and motives rather than resorting to moral demonization, over-generalization, or reduction to hypocrisy. Good practice is to characterize views accurately and sympathetically where reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute moral accusation for argumentative failure
rubrics_metrics.description: When argument fails, resorting to accusations of sin or moral failing (e.g., charging a respondent with 'living in some known and gross sin') is an illegitimate rhetorical move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author uses moral indictment as a rhetorical trump instead of engaging with evidence and reasoning. This is an anti-pattern indicating intellectual weakness and bad faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret texts consistently; avoid ad hoc reinterpretations to fit modern science
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming the Bible contains 'not a single scientific error' while simultaneously reinterpreting Genesis by imaginative hypotheses shows inconsistency: either meaning changes with age or one must provide criteria to decide when reinterpretation is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hermeneutical consistency: if reinterpretation is allowed to reconcile texts with modern knowledge, the work must present a coherent criterion for which passages are elastic and which are not. Avoid using shifting standards that make the text bend to present needs without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular hermeneutics that make doctrine both basis and product of interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'doctrines necessary to salvation' as the test of infallible interpretation while using infallible interpretation to establish which doctrines are necessary is circular and invalidates the interpreter’s claim to a secure basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for circular reasoning in claims of authoritative interpretation. A robust approach supplies independent tests or evidence for interpretive authority rather than relying on self-referential criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate genuine charity in religious instruction; avoid clan-based partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity that is limited to the 'clan' of one’s own party fosters antagonism toward others; love taught as love of the clan is not sympathy toward men as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the moral effect of the teaching: does it increase sympathy and educate the soul, or does it nurture hatred, complacency, and partisan spirit? The ideal is universal sympathy and moral education, not sectarian hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using prophecy/eschatology to inflame partisan or political passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing prophecy mainly to anticipate the downfall of 'enemies' or to advertise pre-millennial triumphs transports political passions onto religion and encourages triumphalism rather than holy spiritual effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether eschatological teaching elevates spiritual life or simply channels partisan animosities into religious rhetoric. Responsible use of prophecy should not be a vehicle for political vengeance or party pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misrepresent scientific or philosophical works through ignorance or hearsay
rubrics_metrics.description: Misstatements about works like the 'Vestiges' or caricaturing philosophers (e.g., Voltaire as simple antitheist) indicate reliance on hearsay or willful ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author has actually engaged with the works he criticizes; fair evaluation requires accurate comprehension. Anti-patterns: imputing positions the authors did not hold, or mistaking nuances for gross errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the pursuit of truth as disinterested; avoid panic-driven defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When belief in certain propositions is treated as indispensable to salvation, anxious haste and alarm 'unman the nature' and preclude calm, disinterested inquiry; panic-driven apologetics are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tone and motive: does the writer encourage calm, honest inquiry, or does the presentation reflect an anxiety for personal or communal survival that biases the examination of evidence? The latter undermines the claim to truth.
